question: Building on the exercise "When SaaS reduces the risk": a small firm currently runs Nextcloud on an IaaS virtual machine and is offered a hosted SaaS file-sharing product instead. Management claims the move would make security "entirely the provider's problem". Using the shared-responsibility model, name two security tasks that would genuinely move to the provider, one responsibility that stays with the firm in either model, and explain — with reference to the Strava case — why management's claim is wrong.
sample_answer: Tasks that move to the provider (any two): OS patching, web-server/TLS configuration, server hardening, firewall management, hardware and hypervisor security. Responsibility that stays: the data row — deciding who may access which data and what shared or published data reveals. The claim is wrong because the data row never leaves the customer's column in the shared-responsibility table, and the Strava case shows a customer-side governance decision failing although no system was breached; no service model makes security entirely somebody else's problem. Grading: two provider-side tasks + the staying responsibility + explicit Strava/data-row argument for full credit.
